what_it_does: When something breaks in a large cloud system — a misconfigured service, a crashing container — engineers must detect the fault, pinpoint which microservice caused it, figure out the root cause, and then fix it. This paper introduces AIOpsLab, an open framework that automates the entire evaluation of AI agents doing that job: it deploys real microservice applications, injects realistic faults, and gives each agent a live cloud environment to interrogate and repair. A 100-problem benchmark reveals that even the best AI agent today solves only 59% of cases.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Existing benchmarks for AI-assisted cloud operations use static datasets — frozen logs, pre-recorded metrics — which do not capture the dynamic, interactive nature of real incidents. AIOpsLab instead lets an AI agent act on a live, running cloud system and get real feedback from each action.

How it works. AIOpsLab has four main parts. (1) A set of cloud applications — realistic microservice systems from open-source benchmarks (social network with 28 microservices, hotel reservation system, astronomy shop, database cluster manager). (2) A fault library that injects two classes of faults: symptomatic faults (like network packet loss or pod crashes) that just degrade the service, and functional faults (like database credential revocation, port misconfiguration, wrong binary in a container) that have a specific, diagnosable root cause. Functional faults are what push agents beyond simple anomaly detection toward root-cause diagnosis and repair. (3) An observability layer that continuously collects logs, distributed traces (Jaeger), and metrics (Prometheus) — the same telemetry a human engineer would use. (4) An Agent-Cloud Interface (ACI) — a clean set of API calls (get_logs, get_metrics, get_traces, exec_shell) that agents use to query the live system, just as a human would type commands.

The key design choice. Separating symptomatic from functional faults. Symptomatic faults cannot be mitigated by addressing a root cause, so they only test detection and localisation. Functional faults have a specific, human-understandable cause, enabling all four levels of the task taxonomy: detect the anomaly, localise the broken microservice, identify the root cause type, and execute the repair.

The benchmark. 100 problems across the four task levels, with 48 selected for the evaluation. Four AI agents were tested: GPT-4 with a shell tool, GPT-3.5 with a shell tool, ReAct (a reasoning-plus-action loop), and FLASH (a workflow-automation agent with hindsight learning).

The result. FLASH achieves the best overall accuracy at 59.3%, getting every detection problem right but struggling at mitigation (54.5%). GPT-3.5 fails every mitigation attempt. Key failure modes: agents call the same API in a loop, get overwhelmed by verbose metric data, or hallucinate non-existent script names. Adding more allowed steps helps FLASH and ReAct but hurts GPT-3.5, suggesting raw reasoning quality matters more than budget.
what_it_does_plain: AIOpsLab is the first evaluation framework that puts AI agents inside a live, real cloud environment — injecting actual faults and measuring whether the agent can find, diagnose, and fix them. It reveals that today's best AI agents correctly handle only about 60% of realistic cloud incidents, and exposes where they fail.
